div.head: Section 225
div.p: SOCRATES. What is the love of gain? What exactly is it, and who are the lovers of gain?
COMRADE. In my opinion, they are those who think it right to make a gain from things of no value.
SOCRATES. Do you mean they do this knowing that the things are of no value, or being ignorant of it? For if they are ignorant, you are calling the lovers of gain foolish.

COMRADE. No, I do not mean they are foolish, but rather crafty and wicked, overpowered by the desire for gain; they know full well that the things from which they dare to make a profit are worth nothing, yet they still dare to love the gain out of shamelessness.

SOCRATES. Do you mean, then, that a lover of gain is someone like a farmer planting a tree, who knows the plant is worthless, but expects to make a profit when it grows up? Is that the sort of person you mean?
COMRADE. The lover of gain, Socrates, thinks he ought to make a profit from everything.

SOCRATES. Do not answer me so recklessly, as if you had suffered some injury, but pay attention and answer me. Do you agree that the lover of gain knows the value of the thing from which he expects to make a profit?
COMRADE. I do.
SOCRATES. Then who is the one who knows the value of plants, and in what season and what soil it is worthwhile to plant them? Let us bring in the experts, just as we would in other matters.
COMRADE. The farmer.
SOCRATES. And by "making a profit," do you mean anything other than getting something more than one has laid out?
COMRADE. That is exactly what I mean.
SOCRATES. Would a farmer, then, knowing that a plant is worthless, and planting it, expect to make a profit?
COMRADE. Certainly not, Socrates.

div.head: Section 226
div.p: SOCRATES. Or do you suppose a horseman who knows a horse is worthless would expect to make a profit by giving it worthless food?
COMRADE. I do not.
SOCRATES. Nor a pilot who furnishes his ship with worthless sails and ropes?
COMRADE. Not at all.
SOCRATES. Nor a general who knows his army is worthless?
COMRADE. By no means.
SOCRATES. Nor a flute-player with worthless flutes, nor a lyre-player with a worthless lyre? Would any of these, knowing their instruments to be worthless, expect to make a profit from them?
COMRADE. Apparently not.

SOCRATES. Then who are these lovers of gain you are talking about? For it surely cannot be these men who, knowing the things to be worthless, yet expect to make a profit from them. And so, my friend, according to your account, there are no lovers of gain anywhere.
COMRADE. But I mean, Socrates, those who, out of insatiable greed, always aim at things that are worthless, and from these things they constantly expect to make a gain.
SOCRATES. But surely not knowing them to be worthless, my excellent friend. For we just proved by argument that this is impossible.
COMRADE. I agree.
SOCRATES. And if they do not know it, it is clear they are ignorant, and they think the worthless things are valuable.
COMRADE. That seems to be the case.
SOCRATES. Now, the lovers of gain love gain, do they not?
COMRADE. Yes.
SOCRATES. And gain, you say, is the opposite of loss?
COMRADE. Yes.
SOCRATES. Is it a good thing for anyone to suffer loss?
COMRADE. For no one.
SOCRATES. Is it a bad thing?
COMRADE. Yes.
SOCRATES. So people are harmed by loss?
COMRADE. They are harmed.
SOCRATES. Loss is therefore an evil?
COMRADE. Yes.
SOCRATES. And gain is the opposite of loss?
COMRADE. Yes.
SOCRATES. So gain is a good thing?
COMRADE. Yes.
SOCRATES. So you are saying that the lovers of gain are those who love the good.
COMRADE. It seems so.
SOCRATES. Well, you are not calling the lovers of gain madmen, my friend. But what about you yourself? Do you love the good, or not?
COMRADE. I do.
SOCRATES. Is there any good thing that you do not love, but rather an evil thing?
COMRADE. No, by Zeus.
SOCRATES. You love all good things alike?
COMRADE. Yes.
SOCRATES. Ask me the same question, and I will also admit that I love the good. But besides you and me, do not all the rest of mankind seem to love the good and hate the evil?
COMRADE. They do appear to.
SOCRATES. And we agreed that gain is a good thing?
COMRADE. We did.
SOCRATES. On this reasoning, then, everyone appears to be a lover of gain; but on the previous reasoning, no one was. So which argument should one follow to avoid making a mistake?

div.head: Section 227
div.p: COMRADE. I think, Socrates, we must understand the lover of gain correctly. The lover of gain is one who is intent on getting it from things from which honorable men do not dare to gain.
SOCRATES. But do you not see, my sweet friend, that we just agreed that to gain is to be benefited?
COMRADE. Yes, what of it?
SOCRATES. Well, we also agreed that all men always wish for good things.
COMRADE. True.
SOCRATES. So do not honorable men also wish to have all gains, since they are good things?
COMRADE. Yes, Socrates, but not gains from which they would suffer harm.
SOCRATES. By "suffer harm," do you mean suffer loss or something else?
COMRADE. No, I mean suffer loss.
SOCRATES. Is a man harmed by gain or by loss?
COMRADE. By loss.
SOCRATES. So it is not possible to be harmed by gain, if indeed gain is good?
COMRADE. Impossible.
SOCRATES. Then the honorable man would not shrink from a gain, if it is genuinely a good thing.
COMRADE. But I say he would shrink from a gain that is wicked.
SOCRATES. Then do you think any gain is wicked, when gain itself has been shown to be good?
COMRADE. I certainly do.
SOCRATES. Then I must try to understand you. Is there such a thing as a wicked gain and a good gain?
COMRADE. I believe so.
SOCRATES. And just as there is good food and bad food, they are both food, are they not?
COMRADE. Yes.
SOCRATES. In the same way, whether a gain is good or bad, is the one any more a gain than the other?
COMRADE. No.
SOCRATES. Let me ask you: if both the good and the bad gain are equally gain, what is the common quality that makes you call them both "gain"?
COMRADE. Because both add to what one had before.
SOCRATES. And you consider this addition to be a good thing, do you not?
COMRADE. I do.
SOCRATES. Then returning to our previous statements, if gain is an addition to one's possessions, and if to have more is a good thing, how can gain be evil?
COMRADE. You confuse me, Socrates.

SOCRATES. But I assure you, I am not trying to deceive you. I am asking you to look at it as if you were examining a coin. If you say one coin is good and another is counterfeit, the counterfeit is still a coin, but it lacks the true value. Now tell me, do you consider the love of gain to be a good thing or a bad thing?
COMRADE. A bad thing, Socrates.

div.head: Section 228
div.p: SOCRATES. You think so? Then let us recall the story of Hipparchus, the son of Peisistratus, who was the eldest and wisest of Peisistratus' sons. He performed many other excellent and wise deeds, and he was the first to bring the poems of Homer into this land, compelling the rhapsodes at the Panathenaea to recite them in sequence, just as they do to this day. He also sent a fifty-oared ship for Anacreon of Teos and brought him to the city, and kept Simonides of Ceos always about him, prevailing upon him with rich rewards and gifts. All these things he did, wishing to educate the citizens, so that he might rule over the best of men, believing that he ought to grudge wisdom to no one, since he was a truly good and noble man.

When the people in the city had been educated by him and marvelled at his wisdom, he proceeded to educate those in the country, setting up herms for them along the roads midway between the city and each deme. Selecting the wisest things he knew, both from others and what he had thought out himself, he put them into elegiac verses and carved them upon the herms as his own poems and displays of wisdom, so that his citizens, while traveling, might read his inscriptions and not wonder at the wise sayings of Delphi, such as "Know thyself" and "Nothing in excess," but might instead consider the sayings of Hipparchus to be wise. Among these inscriptions, one says on the left side of the herm: "A memorial of Hipparchus: walk with just intent." On the right side it says: "A memorial of Hipparchus: deceive not a friend."

Now, this great and wise man Hipparchus was assassinated by Harmodius and Aristogeiton. And the reason for his death was not, as many think, an insult to the sister of Harmodius; that is a foolish tale. The truth is that Harmodius was the beloved of Aristogeiton, and was being educated by him. But Hipparchus also loved Harmodius, and tried to win him away. When Aristogeiton realized this, he killed Hipparchus out of jealousy, much as a rival in love would do.

div.head: Section 229
div.p: SOCRATES. Therefore, we should pay heed to the inscription of Hipparchus, and not deceive a friend. Now, returning to our argument, you say that some gains are good and others bad. But since both are gains, they must share the nature of gain.
COMRADE. Yes, they must.
SOCRATES. And we agreed that to gain is to acquire some good.
COMRADE. We did.
SOCRATES. And all men wish for good things, but they do not wish for bad things.
COMRADE. True.
SOCRATES. If, then, all men wish for good things, and gain is a good thing, then all men must be lovers of gain.
COMRADE. It seems so by this argument, Socrates. I cannot refute it.

SOCRATES. Then it is not right to reproach anyone for being a lover of gain, since everyone loves the good. And if anyone reproaches another for being a lover of gain, he is inadvertently reproaching himself.
COMRADE. I suppose you are right, Socrates.
